title: User interface design in video games (Game Developer)
label: practitioner
claim: Summarises Fagerholt & Lorentzon taxonomy: diegetic/meta/spatial/non-diegetic along two axes (in fiction? in game geometry?). Advice: non-diegetic is the fallback when other forms hurt legibility or consistency; diegetic UI can frustrate when not legible in world geometry.

title: Hodent masterclass listing / Gamer's Brain
label: snippet
claim: Hodent splits game UX into usability (ease of use within human perception/attention/memory limits) and engage-ability (motivation, emotion, game flow). A game can be easy to use and still boring.

title: Idle-game UI growth search results
label: snippet
claim: Idle devs report trimming unused side panels (Miner 2149 devlog), hiding sections until thresholds, and players asking to see upcoming unlock goals to plan; a locked-unlock requirement not matching real appearance confused a player.

title: Game Accessibility Guidelines, Basic tier
label: guideline
claim: Basic tier includes: large well-spaced interactive elements esp. on touch; easily readable default font size; high contrast text/UI vs background; no essential info by fixed colour alone; no essential info by sound alone; progress through text prompts at own pace; start game without multiple menu levels; all UI reachable with the gameplay input method; remap controls; save all settings; simple clear language; avoid flicker. No numeric sizes given.

title: Hoober 2013 (full fetch)
label: research
claim: Field observation: of 1,333 observations, among the 780 users touching the screen, one-handed 49%, cradled 36%, two-handed 15% (90% portrait). Grip changes often, sometimes every few seconds, by task. Author's later comment: people touch the centre of the screen; ignore the reach drawings. No target sizes given.

title: WCAG 2.2 Understanding 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum)
label: guideline
claim: Targets at least 24x24 CSS px, or smaller if a 24px circle centred on each does not intersect another target. Stricter 2.5.5 recommended for important controls. Apple 44pt and Material 48dp were NOT verified from primary pages (fetch returned empty).

title: WCAG 1.4.13 Content on Hover or Focus
label: guideline
claim: Hover/focus-revealed content must be dismissible, hoverable, persistent. Says nothing about touch, where hover does not exist.

title: Into the Breach design postmortem (GDC 2019, Matthew Davis)
label: snippet
claim: Talk listing only. Reviews (not developer) say enemy intents are all shown and outcomes previewed before commitment: perfect information, small numbers.

title: A Dark Room critical analyses
label: opinion
claim: A Dark Room opens with a title, two lines of text, one button; new buttons and text unlock over time so the interface growth mirrors the world; element count grows slowly so players learn each. Risk: minimalism disengages some.

title: Playing to wait: a taxonomy of idle games (CHI 2018)
label: research
claim: Abstract only: analyses play, mechanics, rewards, interactivity, progress rate and user interface of idle games; notes their unusual use of player attention and computer cycles. No interface findings in the abstract.

title: Board Game Arena: tooltips and touchscreen
label: practitioner
claim: Touch users trigger hover tooltips unreliably; proposed fixes: long-press, tap-to-toggle tooltip dismissed by tapping elsewhere, or hiding hover-only tooltips with a hover-capability media query.

title: AppleVis: Kittens Game access
label: verbatim
claim: A VoiceOver user reports browser Kittens Game mouseover text and worker-assign links inaccessible; iOS app better for descriptions.

title: Fix 100vh on mobile viewport
label: practitioner
claim: vh equals the large viewport so 100vh overflows while the mobile address bar shows; dvh tracks the live viewport, svh the smallest. A bottom-pinned bar needs viewport-fit=cover plus env(safe-area-inset-bottom) or env() is zero.

title: NOT FOUND / NULL
label: snippet
claim: Searches for Cookie Clicker / Antimatter Dimensions / Kittens developer accounts of UI growth, Slay the Spire developer reasoning on intent icons, Frostpunk, Darkest Dungeon, gameuidatabase patterns, and primary Apple HIG 44pt / Material 48dp pages returned nothing usable (empty fetch or secondary only). Null, not negative.

title: Apple HIG Accessibility (JSON behind the page)
label: guideline
claim: Table 'Platform / Default control size / Minimum control size': iOS and iPadOS 44x44 pt default, 28x28 pt minimum; macOS 28x28 / 20x20; tvOS 66x66 / 56x56; visionOS 60x60 / 28x28; watchOS 44x44 / 28x28. Also a text-size table: up to 17 pt needs 4.5:1 contrast, 18 pt and bold 3:1.

title: Apple HIG Buttons (JSON behind the page)
label: guideline
claim: 'As a general rule, a button needs a hit region of at least 44x44 pt (in visionOS, 60x60 pt) to ensure that people can select it easily, whether they use a fingertip, a pointer, their eyes, or a remote.'

title: Android: Make apps more accessible
label: guideline
claim: 'For touch interfaces, we recommend that each interactive UI element have a focusable area, or touch target size, of at least 48dpx48dp. Larger is even better.' For precise input (mouse, trackpad) the target can be smaller.

title: Android Accessibility Help: Touch target size
label: guideline
claim: Touch targets include area beyond the visual bounds: an icon may look 24x24dp while padding makes the 48x48dp target. 'Consider making touch targets at least 48x48dp, separated by 8dp of space or more.' Cites the Material Design accessibility guidelines.

title: Hoober 2013 comments: author's later correction
label: verbatim
claim: Hoober, comment of 28 Feb 2017: the reach drawings are 'a bit of a lie because I over-assumed. People touch the center of the screen. More, more quickly, more accurately, and by preference. Not the corners or edges.' 'Please, please everyone ignore those drawings.' Points to later studies that record touch locations directly.

title: Hoober 2017: Design for Fingers, Touch, and People, Part 1
label: research
claim: People shift grip a lot and prefer to view and touch the screen centre. Targets there 'can be smaller, as small as 7 millimeters, while corner target sizes must be about 12 millimeters'; suggested sizes contain only 95% of observed taps. Calls pixel-based standards 'useless' (device pixels bear no relation to human dimensions) and says Google's and Apple's sizes seem based on platform convenience more than human factors. Advice: put dangerous or unrelated items far from others; primary content centre, secondary actions along top and bottom edges.

title: Osmani 2020: Modern Touch-Friendly Design (interview with Hoober)
label: practitioner
claim: Secondary: Hoober's heuristics (people touch the centre, only tap what they see, grip/task/context vary); says avoid the Thumb Zone as a fixed rule; 75% single-thumb figure is misleading next to 49% one-handed grip.

title: WCAG 2.2 Understanding 1.4.13 Content on Hover or Focus
label: guideline
claim: Dismissible: 'A mechanism is available to dismiss the additional content without moving pointer hover or keyboard focus'. Hoverable: 'the pointer can be moved over the additional content without the additional content disappearing'. Persistent: 'remains visible until the hover or focus trigger is removed'. The page frames everything around pointer hover and keyboard focus; touch is not mentioned.

title: Fagerholt & Lorentzon 2009, Beyond the HUD (thesis PDF, sections 7-8)
label: research
claim: The thesis's own design space is two axes: fiction (does it exist in the game's fiction?) and spatiality (is it in the 3D game geometry?); an earlier diegesis x spatiality chart was dropped because diegesis proved 'slightly ambiguous' (blood on screen, Mirror's Edge runner vision). Six categories result: non-diegetic (HUD), meta-perception, meta-representation, geometric, diegetic, signifiers. Hypotheses: more competitive games favour clear overlay HUD ('ambiguous information should be avoided' where decisions must be fast); the closer a world is to plausible reality, the more non-diegetic elements hurt; a world that does not hide being artificial tolerates them. FPS-only scope; guidelines untested beyond small user tests.

title: Hodent: Cognitive psychology applied to UX in video games
label: practitioner
claim: Her own definition: usability is 'removing or at least alleviating all the frustrations and confusion the player could experience while playing the game, if they are not intended by design'; the second component is gameflow (from Sweetser and Wyeth, Csikszentmihalyi), a heuristic set for emotion and motivation. A UX framework is used as a checklist of both.

title: Hodent: 5 misconceptions about UX
label: practitioner
claim: 'one of the UX pillar - usability - is about removing friction and unwanted frustration. It's not about distorting the intended experience'; the second pillar is gameflow, 'how enjoyable and fun the game is'. Her blog index later words the pair as 'usability and engage-ability' (Fortnite post); the book's chapters 11 and 12 are titled Usability and Engage-Ability.

title: CSS Values and Units Module Level 4: viewport-percentage lengths (W3C)
label: guideline
claim: Large viewport (lv*, and default v*) is sized with dynamic UA interfaces retracted: content guaranteed to fill the viewport but 'might be hidden behind such interfaces when they are expanded'. Small viewport (sv*) is sized with them expanded: content fits even when present but 'might not fill the viewport when such interfaces are retracted'. Dynamic viewport (dv*) tracks the interface state and 'can exactly fit within the viewport whether or not such interfaces are present'. Spec: 'The sizes of the dynamic viewport-percentage units are not stable even while the viewport itself is unchanged'; the UA 'is not required to animate' them and may compute as if the interface were fully expanded or retracted during the transition. The reference's claim that dvh can shift layout is therefore normative, not just practitioner opinion. First 100k chars of a 253k-char page read; units text was inside it. Did not read env()/viewport-fit=cover text (a different spec, CSS Environment Variables / Apple).

title: 80.lv: GDC 2019 An Inside Look at Into the Breach (preview)
label: snippet
claim: Preview only: says the talk will address 'which feature to cut'. Nothing on telegraphing or clarity. GDC Vault 1025772 is members-only; no postmortem transcript found anywhere. The Justin Ma 'give up appealing ideas to keep the game clear' line cited in onboarding.jsonl (RPS via repost) was not re-checked.

title: IxDF: Why you'll frustrate players on purpose (Laia Tremosa)
label: practitioner
claim: Author's gloss on Hodent's talk: frustration not by design is a usability problem, 'barriers that prevent players from accessing your intended experience'. This is Tremosa's wording, and the Hodent transcript did not load. It does not contain the reference's quoted 'removing or at least alleviating all the frustrations and confusion' or 'engage-ability'.

title: Hodent, 5 Misconceptions about UX in Video Games (via gamerboom mirror)
label: snippet
claim: Search result only (mirror connection refused): Hodent lists 'UX will distort artistic/design intents' as a misconception; usability is removing friction and frustration, and should not distort the intended experience; Resident Evil table example. Consistent with the reference's 'Usability is not about distorting the intended experience', but I did not read the original and cannot confirm the exact quoted wording. Hodent's two-pillar usability/engage-ability split is repeated in several search results (Gamer's Brain, pocketgamer.biz masterclass piece), still not read at source.

title: Game Accessibility Guidelines, Ensure that all settings are saved/remembered (Basic, General)
label: guideline
claim: Rationale: "Customising lots of settings can be a long winded and difficult task for a wide range of different impairments, as well as a hindrance for everyone else. Remembering settings for subsequent sessions (either at a game level or a platform level) reduces the burden, ensuring that the process only has to be carried out once." Does not say anything about profiles or presets.

title: Game Accessibility Guidelines, Allow the game to be started without the need to navigate through multiple levels of menus (Basic, Cognitive)
label: guideline
claim: Nested menus (team, country, kit selection in a sports game) can be a major obstacle for dyspraxia or short-term memory impairment; pre-game configuration helps many players but a quick-start option opens the game to more; Civilization 5 quick start cited as good example. Not a statement about settings menus specifically; wording paraphrased by the fetch tool, not quoted.

title: Microsoft, Xbox Accessibility Guideline 112: UI navigation (Microsoft Learn, updated 2026)
label: guideline
claim: "Prompting players to configure accessibility settings as the first screen that appears when the game launches" (Minecraft Dungeons example, also reads Xbox platform Ease of Access settings so the screen is read aloud); alternative: meet all XAGs by default at first launch (narration/subtitles on, distractions off). Also: UI fully navigable by keyboard/controller digital input; consistent layout and focus order; text/UI scaling should not force two-direction scrolling (Outer Worlds example); more than one way to find content in complex sets (Minecraft search tab); persistent link back to main menu; encourage an option to disable menu looping. NOTE: this page does NOT itself cover 'persisting settings' or 'previewing'; those are not in XAG 112 as read.

title: Page, Johnsgard, Albert, Allen, User Customization of a Word Processor (CHI '96; authors/title from page, venue from URL)
label: research
claim: 101 self-selected WordPerfect 6.0a for Windows users observed 28 days. 92% customised in some way; "Eighty-six percent ... made changes to their general preference settings"; 25% always show Ruler Bar; 78% left Button Bar at its default top position; 44% removed default buttons (authors suggest "better defaults could have been chosen"); only 4% changed menus; 37% changed backup interval. Shows customisation is NOT rare in this sample, contra the folk claim 'users never change defaults'; but it is a word processor and a self-selected sample, not games.

title: Mackay, Triggers and barriers to customizing software (CHI 1991)
label: snippet
claim: Search result summary: 51 users over four months; most-cited barrier lack of time, then difficulty of customising; triggers include noticing own repeated patterns, fixing something annoying or slow, retrofitting new versions to behave like old (the trigger/barrier summary comes from a later CHI paper, Banovic et al. 2012, as seen in a search snippet). Full PDF not read.

title: Kevin Giguere, Create better game settings options (handy checklist) (Game Developer featured blog, 12 Nov 2018)
label: practitioner
claim: Checklist of yes/no questions, no cited sources, 'based on experience and opinion'. Items: "Can you access the settings before starting a game?"; "Can you modify settings while playing the game?"; "Can you switch between full screen, windowed and borderless?"; "Can you see the effects of screen filters in the menu?"; quality via a single option AND per-element; gamma; master plus individual volumes; rebind keys, "Can you easily reset keybinding?", mouse sensitivity; "Do you have a confirmation message before backing out of options without saving?"; subtitle language separate from audio language; move HUD elements. No TotalBiscuit link; no evidence.

title: Kate Cox, Borderlands 2 really does boast an impressive array of options (Kotaku, 18 Sep 2012)
label: snippet
claim: Only says TotalBiscuit made a video taking "an exhaustive look at the many settings that PC users can tweak to their hearts' delight" in Borderlands 2. Does NOT list which options he praised and quotes none of his words. Evidence he made an options-focused video, nothing about his criteria.

title: troublmaker (blogger), RE: TotalBiscuit on Narrow Field of View (WordPress, 19 Mar 2012)

label: snippet

title: TV Tropes, The Cynical Brit (fan wiki)
label: snippet
claim: Search-tool summary only: he often began new-game videos by going through the options menu and checking for an FOV slider, to viewers' amusement and exasperation; fan-wiki characterisation, not his words. Not opened.

title: Regen7, TotalBiscuit won't be happy with this options menu (Steam discussion, Planetbase, 15 Oct 2015)
label: opinion

title: Peter 'Durante' Thoman, Trails of Cold Steel PC Guest Blog #2: Graphical Enhancements & Options (XSEED/Marvelous USA, 26 Jul 2017)
label: developer
claim: Port developer on his own launcher: "Every single option has a description text, and often it also shows visual comparisons of the settings (on the right)"; "The entire launcher ... can be navigated just using a gamepad"; frame-rate options 30 / 60 / unlimited, unlimited offered on a "your own risk" basis (not fully QA'd); FoV larger "desirable" close to a large monitor; MSAA 2x/4x/8x; AF a single checkbox because "there's no reason to bother with less than 16xAF". Shows a deliberate choice to collapse options with no useful range. One port, one developer; not evidence players use descriptions.

title: Matthew Dunnerstick, Naughty Dog, The Last of Us Part II: Accessibility Features Detailed (Naughty Dog blog, 9 Jun 2020)
label: developer

The post does NOT say whether a first-boot prompt exists (fetch tool: 'doesn't say'); second-hand search summaries also found none, so first-boot prompt is unverified for TLOU2.

title: GameSpot, The Many Ways The Last Of Us 2 Is Designed To Be Accessible (2020)
label: snippet
claim: Search summary: Emilia Schatz quoted (from a Verge interview) "Accessibility for us is about removing barriers that are keeping players from completing a game"; options not about 'dumbing down'; 60+ options. Not opened.

label: snippet
claim: Two fetches returned only the title (truncated). From a search summary: lists features PC gamers expect and recommends 'sane default settings based on the users' hardware, at minimum native resolution'. Author/date/TB link unknown. Not usable beyond a lead.

FoV slider has both vertical AND horizontal numbers', so he checked both mouse acceleration and FOV number format). label: guideline

Apple platforms only; no Android/Google source found. Says nothing on previews, revert timers or presets.

claim: Search summary: reports should screenshot and describe video settings, note a missing FOV slider in first/third-person games (own FoV subsection), average framerates graph, controls section where 'mouse acceleration and keyboard customization' are tested; Input settings table value 'true' means a visible in-game or bundled-launcher option, 'hackable' for tweakable by file. Page and the infobox template were Cloudflare-blocked to fetch and curl. Exact PCGamingWiki field list is unverified.

title: Digital Foundry on settings-menu design (Battaglia: descriptions, previews, VRAM meters)
label: null
claim: Queries run: DF PC settings menu descriptions/preview/VRAM meter/performance impact; DF Spider-Man Remastered PC settings menu praised; DF Alex Battaglia settings menu VRAM meter Gears 5 RDR2 (extended). Result: only secondary guides/forum posts; no DF or Battaglia statement praising settings descriptions or previews was found, and Gears 5 returned nothing. The claim that DF praised settings descriptions is unverified, not refuted. label: null

label: snippet
claim: Bug-tracker snippets: 15 seconds is a common revert window (Mint proposal, Sony Windows support article); users complain the timer is too short to check the display; a KDE bug argues time-out should revert rather than keep the new setting. Desktop OS user complaints, not game guidance or research. No game-specific source for apply/revert found.

title: TotalBiscuit, What a PC Options menu is supposed to look like (YouTube, 2012-09-18)
label: practitioner
claim: Walks Borderlands 2's options as a model PC menu: FOV slider 70-110 ('90 is what I would consider to be industry standard for PC'); full resolution list; HUD scale and bounds adjustable because console HUDs are sized for a TV 'half the room away'; UI sway toggle; windowed mode, vsync; frame cap 30/50/60/72/120/unlimited; 16x anisotropic; settings auto-detected from hardware; granular graphics options; mute when minimised; VOIP levels, push-to-talk; separate music/effects/dialogue levels; subtitles on by default; training messages can be turned off; aim toggle vs hold; mouse smoothing off by default ('quite frankly terrible'); invert mouse; full key rebinding with reset. 'I haven't seen an options menu like that for a very very long time in a AAA release.' One game's menu, not a general checklist.

title: TotalBiscuit, GTA V - Port Report (YouTube, 2015-04-16)
label: practitioner
claim: Notes key rebinding, raw mouse input by default and no mouse acceleration; an in-menu video-memory meter that over-reported under SLI ('that's not how SLI works'); settings that cause hitching or big VRAM jumps; FOV 'still a little bit narrow even at maximum'. Only excerpts read.

title: PCGamingWiki, PC Report guide (community blog)
label: practitioner
claim: Structure for a PC port report: Video settings ('Be sure to mention lack of features like field of view slider in first/third person games, lack of resolutions in mobile ports'; FoV gets its own subsection); Performance analysis per effect; Controls ('be sure to test mouse acceleration and keyboard customization', controller mapping optional); Audio ('check subtitles, closed captions options and volume sliders', surround). A reviewing guide, 'not set of rules'; says nothing about menu usability (descriptions, previews).

title: Mackay, Triggers and Barriers to Customizing Software (CHI 1991)
label: research
claim: Sample/method: 51 staff of MIT Project Athena (managers 10, secretaries 5, systems programmers 12, applications programmers 8, other staff 16), mixed technical levels, using customizable Unix/X Window software; data collected 'over a period of four months' via two interviews per person, a two-page questionnaire, copies of customization files, plus automatic records; critical-incident technique. Self-reported reasons coded from open-ended interviews; participants 'were not given this list'. No game context.

title: Mackay, Triggers and Barriers to Customizing Software (CHI 1991)
label: research
claim: Triggers/barriers (Table 3, % of 51 users): 96% (49/51) cited at least one trigger, 31 unique, 226 total, mean 4.4/person. Top triggers: 'Retrofit when system changed' 43%, 'Notice own repeated patterns' 43%, 'When it gets too annoying' 41%, 'I see something neat' 39%, 'Something breaks' 29%, 'Learn new system' 25%, 'Setup for me when I arrived' 25%, 'Switch environments' 25%. 92% (47/51) cited at least one barrier, 20 unique, 102 total, mean 2. Barriers: 'Lack of time' 63% ('by far the biggest'), 'Too hard to modify' 33%, 'System upgrade broke things' 12%, 'I'm not interested' 12%, 'Poor documentation' 10%, 'Lack isn't painful enough' 10%, 'I'm rooted in my old patterns' 8%, 'I don't know the possibilities' 6%, 'I'm afraid to risk it' 6%. Text: 'One third cited lack of knowledge about how to make desired customizations (33%)'; 'Lack of time often means that the user is not willing to risk spending an unknown amount of time'.

title: Mackay, Triggers and Barriers to Customizing Software (CHI 1991)
label: research
claim: Frequency/defaults/upgrades: Customizing ranged 'from once every six months to every few days. However, users still spend most of their time simply "using" the software'; 'Usually, users need a reason to customize'. Abstract: 'simply providing a set of customization features does not ensure that users will take advantage of' them; 'many people do not take advantage of the customization features at all'. No percentage who kept defaults and no count of customizers vs non-customizers is reported. Upgrades: users 'often customize to maintain a stable interaction with the software, rather than to take advantage of new features'; all who customized included stability-keeping customizations, retrofitting the new software 'to be like the old' or refusing it; 4% 'Avoid software to avoid retrofit'; 'System upgrade broke things' is a 12% barrier. Most likely to be worth it: customizations that let users 'continue working as they did before' or automate a repeated action with one command; key bindings 'very resistant to change'; aesthetic customizations 'generally avoided' unless bored. Users 'satisfice' rather than optimize. Cites Mackay 1988a: 50% of 1.5+-year secretary text-editor users had not learned cut and paste.

title: Mackay, Triggers and Barriers to Customizing Software (CHI 1991)
label: research
claim: Bearing on the rule 'Users do change settings: 92% of 101 (Page et al. 1996)... nobody changes defaults is folklore': Mackay QUALIFIES, does not contradict or directly support. She gives no customizer-vs-defaulter rate (her 96% / 92% figures are triggers/barriers cited, not people who customized; do not conflate with Page's 92%). Her point is that customizing is conditional on a trigger (breakage, annoyance, repeated pattern, system change, seeing a colleague's setup) and blocked mostly by time (63%) and difficulty (33%), so defaults carry most use ('most of their time simply using'). Sample is 51 MIT/Athena staff in 1991 on Unix, not games. Game-relevant inferences (not Mackay's): trigger moments are annoyance, breakage and an update changing things; 'Setup for me when I arrived' (25%) and 'I see something neat' (39%) suggest shared presets and seen-elsewhere settings drive change; 6% did not know options existed and 33% found them too hard to modify (discoverability); 'Lack of time' 63% means a cheap, fast settings flow; 43% retrofit after a system change and 12% upgrade-broke-it means preserve settings and keybinds across patches. Nothing on first-launch settings screens specifically.
